title: How to Convert a Finance Manager Salary from Hourly to Annual
description: Learn how to convert a finance manager salary from hourly to annual using the 38-hour week formula, including tax, super, and award rates from Fair Work Ombudsman.
salarySummary: Based on ABS average weekly earnings, a finance manager salary equates to roughly $54.83 per hour for a 38-hour week, or $108,352 annually before tax and super.

faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time role, assume 38 hours per week. For example, $54.83 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $108,352 per year. This formula works for any hourly rate, but remember it assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. The national minimum wage for casuals is $33.05 per hour (including loading). When using our timesheet tool, check the 'casual loading' box to add 25% to your base rate. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my salary?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your salary at 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For a $108,352 annual salary, super would be an additional $13,002.24. This is not deducted from your pay; your employer pays it into your super fund.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Annual Pay Formula

To convert an hourly rate to an annual salary, use this simple formula: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super. For full-time work, we assume a standard 38-hour week, as set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If you work part-time or casual, adjust the hours accordingly.

For example, if you earn $54.83 per hour (the approximate rate for a finance manager based on ABS average weekly earnings), your annual salary would be $54.83 × 38 × 52 = $108,352. This calculation is the same whether you're paid weekly, fortnightly, or monthly. A fortnightly pay period is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two.

## The National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

Australia has a National Minimum Wage (NMW) that applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026, the NMW is **$26.44 per hour** for full-time and part-time employees, or **$1,004.90 per week** for 38 hours. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making their minimum rate **$33.05 per hour**.

However, most employees are covered by a modern award that sets higher minimum rates. For finance roles, the **Banking, Finance and Insurance Award** [MA000019] applies. This award has specific classification levels and pay rates that are generally above the NMW. You can find the latest pay guide on the Fair Work Ombudsman website. Always check the award that covers your job to ensure you're being paid correctly.

## What About a Finance Manager Salary?

If you're researching a **finance manager salary**, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) provides a useful benchmark. As of May 2026, **average weekly earnings for full-time adult employees in ordinary time** were **$2,083.70 per week**. This translates to an annual salary of about **$108,352** (based on 52 weeks). For a 38-hour week, that's roughly **$54.83 per hour**.

Keep in mind that this is an average across all full-time adults, not specific to finance managers. Actual salaries vary by experience, location, and employer. Some finance managers may be covered by an enterprise agreement that offers higher pay. Use the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page for more industry-specific data.

## Tax and Superannuation

Your gross annual salary is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) applies a progressive tax scale for 2026–27:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus, a **2% Medicare levy** generally applies (with reductions for low-income earners). For a $108,352 salary, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be around $24,000–$25,000, leaving a take-home pay of about $83,000–$84,000. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a detailed breakdown.

**Superannuation** is paid on top of your salary. The super guarantee is **12% of your ordinary earnings**, up to the **maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year**. For a $108,352 salary, your employer would contribute an additional $13,002.24 to your super fund. This is not deducted from your pay; it's an extra cost for the employer. Learn more on the [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page.

## Using the Timesheet Tool

Our [timesheet](/) tool helps you convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures. Simply enter your base hourly rate. If you're a casual employee, check the **casual loading box** to add 25% on top. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – the tool handles that for you. The tool also estimates tax and super based on the latest ATO rates.

For award-specific rates, refer to the [pay guides](/blog) on our site, which link to the Fair Work Ombudsman's official documents. You can also check the [reference tables](/data) for historical rates and the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for current NMW figures.

## Important Notes

This estimate assumes the same hourly rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates or allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds (2026–27 thresholds not yet confirmed). HELP loans, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your actual pay or tax.

For personalised advice, consult a qualified accountant or the ATO.
